We have mass spec m/z 268.1939 (M+?), likely molecular weight ~268. The proton NMR shows signals: 2.22 (s, 6H), 2.32 (s, 6H), 4.46 (d, J=4.8 Hz, 2H), 7.06 (ddd, 8H). So total protons integrated: 6+6+2+8 = 22 H. So formula C? H22? N? O? The mass 268 suggests maybe C18H22NO (calc mass: C18=216, H22=22, N=14, O=16 total = 268). Yes matches. So formula C18H22NO. Good.

Carbon NMR shows 18 carbons: aromatic many around 124-135 (12 aromatic carbons?), plus 62.10 (2), 34.50 (2), 19.40 (2). So likely two equivalent aromatic rings? 12 aromatic carbons suggests two phenyl rings (each 6). The aromatic protons 8H suggests two para-disubstituted phenyl rings (each 4 H). The aromatic carbon signals: pairs duplicate (two each). So symmetric molecule with two identical phenyl groups.

Aliphatic: 4.46 d (2H) likely CH2 attached to heteroatom (maybe CH2-O or CH2-N). 2.22 s 6H and 2.32 s 6H likely two equivalent methyl groups each 6H (i.e., two gem-dimethyl groups? Actually each 6H suggests two equivalent methyl groups each 3H but integration 6H means two methyl groups overlapping. So total 4 methyl groups? Wait 6H each = two methyl groups overlapping? Could be two equivalent dimethyl groups (i.e., two sets of two methyls). So maybe a tert-butyl? But tert-butyl would be 9H. So maybe two isopropyl? But isopropyl gives 6H (CH3)2 and a CH at ~2-3 ppm. Not present. So maybe two N,N-dimethyl groups? N,N-dimethyl gives 6H singlet. Two such groups would give 12H total, but we have two singlets each 6H, so two N,N-dimethyl groups attached to different nitrogens? But only one N in formula.

Maybe the molecule is N,N-diethyl? That gives 4H quartet etc. Not.

Consider structure: maybe N-methyl-N-ethyl? Not.

We have 2.22 and 2.32 both singlets 6H each: could be two equivalent aromatic methyl groups (para to something) on phenyl rings: e.g., p-xylene moieties each have two methyls (4 methyls total 12H). But each aromatic ring would have two methyls (para positions) giving 6H each? Actually each ring with two methyls gives 6H total (two methyl groups 3+3). But they would be chemically equivalent? If symmetric, both methyls on each ring may be equivalent? In p-xylene, the two methyls are equivalent, giving 6H singlet. So each phenyl ring could be p-xylene (i.e., 1,4-dimethylbenzene). Two such rings would give two singlets each 6H. Good.

Then aromatic protons: each p-xylene has 4 aromatic protons (two sets equivalent) giving 4H per ring, total 8H, matches 7.06 ddd (maybe pattern). So aromatic part fits.

Now aliphatic CH2 at 4.46 d (2H) attached to O or N. Likely O-CH2- linking the two rings? Could be a benzylic CH2 attached to oxygen (e.g., O-CH2-Ph). The carbon shift 62 ppm matches O-CH2. So maybe a benzylic ether linking the two p-xylene rings? But we have only one O.

Structure could be: (p-xylene)CH2-O-CH2-(p-xylene)? That would have two CH2 groups, but we only see one CH2 (2H). So maybe only one CH2 attached to O, and the other connection is via nitrogen? N attached to aromatic carbon? But N is only one.

Consider N-methyl? No.

Maybe the molecule is a benzyl dimethylamine? But we have two aromatic rings.

Possibility: N,N-dimethyl-4-(p-tolyl)benzylamine? That would have N(CH3)2 (6H singlet) and a p-tolyl (CH3 3H) not 6H.

Our data: two 6H singlets suggests two N,N-dimethyl groups? But only one N.

Could be N,N-diethyl? Not.

Maybe the molecule is a benzylic ether of p-xylene: p-xylene-CH2-O-CH2-p-xylene? That would have two CH2 (both O-CH2) giving two signals maybe overlapping? But we only see one CH2.

Maybe the CH2 is attached to N (N-CH2-Ph) giving shift ~45 ppm not 62.

Thus O-CH2-Ph is plausible.

What about formula: C18H22NO includes one N and one O. If we have two p-xylene rings (C8H10 each) that's C16H20. Add CH2 (C1H2) gives C17H22. Need N and O left: maybe N attached to O as N-oxide? Not.

Alternatively, maybe the molecule is N-methyl-4-(p-tolyl)benzylamine? Let's compute: p-tolyl (C7H7) plus benzyl (C7H7) plus NCH3 (CH3) gives C15H17N? Not.

Let's compute formula for p-xylene (C8H10). Two of them = C16H20. Add CH2 (C1H2) = C17H22. Need N and O: add NO gives C17H22NO, but we have C18. So need one more carbon. Could be a carbonyl? But O present.

Maybe structure: p-xylene-CH2-O-CH2-p-xylene? That adds two CH2 (C2H4) to C16H20 => C18H24, too many H and O2.

Our formula C18H22NO suggests one O, one N, 18 carbons, 22 H. Aromatic rings 12 carbons (two phenyl) = C12H8 (since each phenyl has 5 H, but we have 8 H aromatic). Actually each phenyl ring with two methyl substituents (p-xylene) has C8H10. Two such = C16H20. Leaves C2H2NO. The remaining atoms: CH2 (C1H2) attached to O (makes O-CH2-). Then N attached maybe as -NH-? N with one H? But we have no extra H beyond 22 accounted? Let's count: C16H20 from rings, plus CH2 gives C17H22, need one more carbon and N and O. Could be carbonyl C=O attached to N (amide) linking to CH2? But O already used.

Maybe structure: p-xylene-CO-NH-CH2-p-xylene? That would have carbonyl O, N, CH2. Carbonyl carbon adds C1O1, N adds N1, CH2 adds C1H2. Total extra C2H2NO. So overall C18H22NO. Yes! So could be a benzyl amide linking two p-xylene groups: p-xylene carbonyl (p-toluic acid?) Actually p-xylene-CO- is p-toluic acid? Wait p-xylene is dimethylbenzene. p-toluic acid is methylbenzoic acid (C8H8O2). Not.

But we need carbonyl attached to aromatic ring (aryl carbonyl). So maybe 4,4'-dimethylbenzophenone? That's C15H12O? Not.

Our structure: 4,4'-dimethylbenzoyl? Let's think: 4,4'-dimethylbenzophenone would be (p-tolyl)-(C=O)-(p-tolyl). That formula C15? Actually each p-tolyl C8H7 (since one H replaced by carbonyl). Two = C16H14, plus carbonyl carbon O gives C17H14O. Not.

Our formula includes N, so maybe it's an amide: p-tolyl-CO-NH-CH2-p-tolyl? That would have one CH2 attached to aromatic ring (benzyl). The CH2 attached to N would be around 3-4 ppm maybe 4.46 d (attached to N?). But N-CH2 attached to aromatic maybe 3.5. O-CH2 attached to carbonyl? Not.

But 4.46 d suggests CH2 attached to heteroatom (O or N) and coupled to something (maybe CH2 next to N?). J=4.8 small, maybe coupling to NH? Could be CH2 attached to N (N-CH2) coupling to NH (1H) small.

We have only one CH2 signal, integration 2H, doublet.

Thus likely CH2 attached to N (N-CH2-Ph) where the NH is not observed (maybe exchange). So N is secondary amine (NH-CH2-Ph). The CH2 attached to aromatic gives shift ~3.5-4.5 if attached to N? Could be 4.46.

Thus structure: N-(p-tolyl)-p-tolylmethanamine? Actually N attached to aromatic carbonyl? Not.

Consider N-(p-tolyl)benzylamine? That would have one p-tolyl (C8H9) and one benzyl (C7H7) plus NHCH2? Not.

But we have two p-xylene rings (each C8H10). If one is attached via carbonyl to N (amide) and the other via CH2 to N (benzyl amine). So structure: p-tolyl-CO-NH-CH2-p-tolyl. That matches formula: each p-tolyl (C8H7) after substitution? Let's compute: p-tolyl (C7H7CH3) = C8H9? Actually tolyl (C7H7-CH3) is C8H9? Wait phenyl C6H5, add CH3 at para gives C7H7? Actually p-tolyl group attached via carbonyl: C6H4(CH3) (since one H replaced by carbonyl). That's C7H7. Two such groups: C14H14. Add carbonyl carbon O: C15H14O. Add NH (adds N and H): C15H15NO. Add CH2 (C1H2) attached to second aromatic? Wait the second aromatic already attached via carbonyl? Hmm.

Let's compute more systematically: Structure: 4-methylbenzoyl (p-tolyl carbonyl) attached to NH-CH2-4-methylphenyl. So left side: carbonyl carbon attached to aromatic ring (C6H4CH3) = C7H7 (since carbonyl carbon not part of aromatic). Actually the carbonyl carbon is separate: the carbonyl carbon is part of the amide, attached to aromatic ring. So left aromatic ring: C7H7 (C6H4CH3). Carbonyl carbon adds C1O1. So left side contributes C8H7O. Then NH adds N and H. Then CH2 adds C1H2. Then right aromatic ring (p-tolyl) attached via CH2 (benzyl) so aromatic ring is C7H7 (C6H4CH3). Total: Carbons: 8+1+7 = 16? Wait compute: left aromatic C7, carbonyl C1 =8, CH2 C1 =9, right aromatic C7 =16. Need 18 carbons, missing 2. Maybe each aromatic ring is dimethyl (two methyls) not one. So p-xylene (C8H9?) Actually p-xylene (1,4-dimethylbenzene) formula C8H10. When attached via carbonyl, one methyl remains, the other position is carbonyl, so aromatic part becomes C8H9? Let's compute: p-xylene has C8H10. Replace one hydrogen (para) with carbonyl (C=O) gives C8H9O? Actually carbonyl carbon is external, so aromatic part loses one H, becomes C8H9. Good. The other p-xylene attached via CH2 loses one H (the benzylic position) becomes C8H9 as well. So total carbons: 8+8 =16 plus carbonyl carbon =1 => 17. Still missing 1 carbon. Maybe there is an extra methyl on nitrogen (N-methyl). That would add CH3 (C1H3). Then total C18, H? Let's compute H: each p-xylene originally C8H10. After substitution each loses 1 H, so each becomes C8H9. Two give C16H18. Add carbonyl carbon no H. Add CH2 (2 H) gives C17H20. Add N-methyl (CH3) gives C18H23, plus NH? Actually N now tertiary (no H). So H23, but formula H22. So maybe N is secondary (has H) not methyl. Then we have N-H (1 H) instead of methyl. That gives H22. So structure: 4,4'-dimethylbenzoyl-NH-CH2-4-methylphenyl. That matches formula C18H22NO. Good.

Thus SMILES: For left aromatic: Cc1ccc(cc1)C(=O)N? Actually carbonyl attached to aromatic: O=Cc1ccc(C)cc1? Wait carbonyl attached to aromatic carbon (aryl carbonyl). SMILES: O=Cc1ccc(C)cc1N? But N attached to carbonyl as amide: O=Cc1ccc(C)cc1N? Then N attached to CH2-aryl: NCC? Actually N attached to CH2 which attached to second aromatic: NCH2c2ccc(C)cc2. So full SMILES: O=Cc1ccc(C)cc1NCCc2ccc(C)cc2. Need to ensure CH2 is attached to aromatic carbon (benzyl). So N-CH2-Ph. So SMILES: O=Cc1ccc(C)cc1NCCc2ccc(C)cc2. Count atoms: carbonyl C=O plus aromatic left C8, right C8, CH2 (C) plus N. Carbons: carbonyl carbon (1) + left aromatic 8 + right aromatic 8 + CH2 (1) = 18. Hydrogens: left aromatic after substitution has 9 H? Actually left aromatic has methyl (CH3) and 4 aromatic H (since carbonyl replaces one). So left: CH3 (3) + aromatic H (4) =7. Right aromatic similar: CH3 (3) + aromatic H (4) =7. CH2 (2). NH (1). Total H =7+7+2+1=17? Wait missing. Let's compute formula from SMILES using tool.
